title: Israel’s President Chooses Eisenkot Over Netanyahu to Lead Next Government, Al Jazeera Reports
body:
Israel’s president has handed former chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot a 28‑day mandate to assemble a coalition that can command a majority of 61 seats in the 120‑member Knesset, effectively bypassing longtime rival Benjamin Netanyahu in the race to become the next prime minister. The decision, announced by President Isaac Herzog on Saturday, signals a decisive shift in the country’s political calculus after three consecutive inconclusive elections left the nation mired in deadlock.

Herzog’s choice reflects the growing consensus among centrist and right‑leaning parties that Eisenkot, a respected military veteran with a reputation for discipline and cross‑factional networking, offers a more viable path to stability than the polarising figure of Netanyahu, who has dominated Israeli politics for more than a decade. The president’s remarks underscored the urgency of forming a government capable of addressing pressing domestic challenges – from soaring housing costs and a strained welfare system to the looming threat of renewed conflict with Hamas – while also navigating a fragile coalition landscape that includes ultra‑Orthodox parties, Arab representatives and centrist blocs.

Eisenkot, 59, served as chief of the General Staff of the Israel Defense Forces from 2015 to 2019 and is widely regarded as a pragmatic leader who can bridge ideological divides. In his brief response to Herzog, he pledged to work “with all responsible parties” to craft a coalition that respects democratic norms and security imperatives. Analysts note that his military background may appeal to right‑wing factions such as Likud’s hardliners and the religious Zionist camp, while his comparatively moderate public persona could make him acceptable to centrist parties like Yesh Atid and the newly formed “New Hope” movement, which have been looking for an alternative to Netanyahu’s hard‑line approach.

The move also reshapes the strategic calculations of Netanyahu’s Likud, which entered the latest election hoping to retain power by forming a coalition with smaller right‑wing and religious parties. Netanyahu’s refusal to step aside, despite the president’s invitation to another candidate, has intensified internal party tensions. Some Likud lawmakers have begun quietly reaching out to Eisenkot’s camp, weighing the benefits of joining a broader government versus remaining in opposition. Should Eisenkot succeed, Netanyahu could find himself relegated to a junior ministerial role or forced into an extended period of political marginalisation, a scenario that would mark a historic downturn for a leader who has served as prime minister for a total of 15 years.

International observers are watching the development closely, as Israel’s political stability has direct implications for regional security and diplomatic initiatives, including the tentative normalization talks with Saudi Arabia and the ongoing negotiations over a ceasefire in Gaza. A government led by Eisenkot might be more inclined to pursue a balanced foreign policy, leveraging his security credentials to maintain strong ties with the United States while also seeking to de‑escalate tensions with neighbouring states. Conversely, a coalition dominated by hard‑line religious parties could reinforce a more confrontational stance, complicating peace efforts and potentially drawing criticism from European partners.

The 28‑day deadline places considerable pressure on Eisenkot to navigate a fragmented parliamentary landscape, where no single party holds a clear majority. He must secure the support of at least three additional parties beyond his own centrist bloc, a task that will likely involve complex negotiations over budget allocations, defense spending, and contentious social issues such as conscription for ultra‑Orthodox yeshiva students. The president’s decision also serves as a reminder of Israel’s semi‑presidential system, wherein the head of state can influence the composition of the executive by selecting a candidate deemed most capable of forming a functional government.

As the clock ticks down, Israel stands at a crossroads. Eisenkot’s ability to forge a cohesive coalition could usher in a period of renewed governance and policy continuity, addressing the electorate’s fatigue after three elections in less than two years. Failure to do so, however, may trigger yet another round of voting, prolonging political paralysis and deepening public disillusionment. The coming weeks will reveal whether Israel’s political establishment can coalesce around a leader who blends military experience with a pragmatic approach to coalition‑building, setting the stage for the country’s domestic agenda and its role on the volatile Middle‑East stage.
